Calculate linkage disequilibrium between SNPs

Source: R/ld.R
calc_ld.Rd

Calculates r², a measure of linkage disequilibrium (LD), between every pair of SNPs in the data.

Usage

calc_ld(x, max_snps = 300)

Arguments

x

A snpscape object.

max_snps

Maximum number of SNPs to use.

Value

A tibble with one row per pair of SNPs: snp1, snp2 (SNP IDs), pos1, pos2 (positions), index1, index2 (the SNPs' order along the chromosome) and r2.

Details

What LD is

Chromosomes are passed from parents to children in long pieces, which are broken up only occasionally by recombination. SNPs that are close together therefore tend to be inherited together, so knowing a person's genotype at one SNP tells you something about their genotype at a nearby SNP. This non-random association is called linkage disequilibrium.

r² is the squared correlation between the genotypes at two SNPs across people: 0 means no association, 1 means one SNP perfectly predicts the other. LD typically decays with distance, but the pattern is patchy: "blocks" of high LD are separated by recombination hotspots.

LD differs between populations. African populations, which have the longest history and largest long-term population sizes, generally show shorter stretches of LD than populations that went through bottlenecks during migrations out of Africa. A recent selective sweep (as around LCT in Europeans) creates an unusually long stretch of high LD, because the favoured allele rose in frequency so fast that recombination had little time to break up the surrounding chromosome. Compare populations by using keep_pops() before calc_ld().

Practicalities

Rare SNPs give unreliable r² values, so filter them out first, e.g. with filter_snps(min_maf = 0.05) (and without LD pruning, which would remove exactly the pattern you want to see). The number of pairs grows quickly with the number of SNPs, so if there are more than max_snps SNPs, an evenly spaced subset is used.

Examples

example_lct |>
  filter_snps(min_maf = 0.05) |>
  keep_pops(super_pop = "EUR") |>
  calc_ld()
